etymology: Hebrew yashob‘am, “the people return” or “dwelling among the people,” the chief of David’s captains, a Hachmonite, set over the first monthly course of the host.
biblical_def: Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel was the chief of David’s captains, set over the course of the first month, of four and twenty thousand men in his division (1Ch 27:2-3). He is the same who is called the chief among the mighty men in the Chronicler’s roll, who lifted up his spear against three hundred and slew them at one time (1Ch 11:11). His name signifies “dwelling among the people,” and he stood foremost of that valiant company who hazarded their lives for David and helped to establish his throne. The dictionary honours that Jashobeam was not only mighty in the day of battle but ordered in the day of peace, taking his appointed month and serving the king in his course; for the kingdom of David is no chaos of free swords, but a host marshalled rank by rank under the anointed head. There is a figure here of the warfare of the saints under great David’s greater Son, the Lord Jesus Christ, in whose army each is given his station and his season. Jashobeam stands as a witness that valour is perfected in submission, that the strongest arm is laid most willingly under the rule of the king. He who was chief of the captains held his place by appointment and not by self-will, and so the saint, however gifted, serves Christ in the order his Captain assigns, that the whole body might move as one under its Head.

etymology: Hebrew doday, “beloved” or “loving,” an Ahohite, captain of the second monthly course of David’s host, the father of Eleazar the mighty man.
biblical_def: Dodai the Ahohite, also called Dodo, was set over the course of the second month in the ordering of David’s army, of four and twenty thousand men (1Ch 27:4). He was the father of Eleazar, one of the three mightiest of David’s men, who smote the Philistines until his hand was weary and clave unto the sword, so that the LORD wrought a great victory that day (2Sa 23:9). His name signifies “beloved,” and he stood high among the valiant, both for his own captaincy and for the renown of the son he begat. The dictionary honours that Dodai held his appointed month in the host, taking his place in the ordered ranks that David set in their courses; for the kingdom of the anointed was no rabble of warriors but a host marshalled under the head. There is a sweetness in his name, beloved, that befits the company of the king, for these mighty men loved David and hazarded their lives for him in the day of his distress. Dodai stands as a witness that to be beloved and to be faithful go together in the service of the king, and that the love which the saints bear to Christ the greater David is proved in steadfast service in the rank He appoints. The father who served in his course begat a son who clave unto the sword; so a faithful generation passes on its valour, and the LORD is glorified in both.

etymology: Hebrew shammoth, “desolations” or “ruins,” a Harorite, captain of the fifth monthly course of David’s host, also called Shammah and Shamhuth.
biblical_def: Shammoth the Izrahite was set over the course of the fifth month in the ordering of David’s army, of four and twenty thousand men (1Ch 27:8). He is the same who is called Shammoth the Harorite among the mighty men in one roll, and Shammah the Harodite in the book of Samuel, the variation of the name belonging to the manner of the lists rather than to any confusion of the man (1Ch 11:27; 2Sa 23:25). His name signifies “desolations,” a stern word, yet borne by a soldier set to keep order in the host of the anointed. The dictionary honours that Shammoth, whatever the spelling under which his name is preserved, was numbered among the valiant and given his month to serve in his course. There is comfort here for the reader who finds the same man written under differing forms, for the Spirit of God who kept the record permits no real loss; the man is one, the witness sure. Shammoth stands as a figure of the saint who serves under the King though the world scarce remembers his name aright, content that his Master knows him. For the kingdom of David is an image of the kingdom of Christ, in which each soldier is marshalled to his station, and the LORD who set Shammoth over the fifth course is the same who orders the warfare of His people and forgets not the least of those who keep their rank for Him.

biblical_def: Helez the Pelonite was set over the course of the seventh month in the ordering of David’s army, of four and twenty thousand men, and is reckoned of the children of Ephraim (1Ch 27:10). He is named among David’s mighty men in both rolls, called the Pelonite by the Chronicler and the Paltite in the book of Samuel, the same valiant man under the two forms of the name (1Ch 11:27; 2Sa 23:26). His name perhaps signifies “strength,” a fitting word for a soldier of the king’s chosen company, yet of his own particular exploits the Scripture is silent. The dictionary honours that Helez served faithfully in his appointed course, neither first nor most renowned of the thirty, but steadfast in his place, taking his month and keeping his rank in the host. There is a pattern of grace here, for the kingdom of David is a figure of the kingdom of great David’s greater Son, and the men who held their station in his army are an image of those who serve Christ each in his own order. Helez stands as a witness that faithfulness in an assigned station, though it win no song of its own, is honoured by the LORD; for it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful, and the good and faithful servant, however quiet his labour, shall hear his Master’s Well done in the day of reckoning.

biblical_def: Ira the son of Ikkesh the Tekoite was set over the course of the sixth month in the ordering of David’s army, of four and twenty thousand men (1Ch 27:9). He is named among the mighty men of David in both rolls, the son of a man of Tekoa, that town of the hill country of Judah whence came also the wise woman who pleaded before the king, and whence in later days the prophet Amos was called from the herdmen (1Ch 11:28; 2Sa 23:26). His name signifies “watchful,” a fitting word for a soldier set to guard his lord and to keep his appointed watch in the host. Of his own exploits the Scripture says nothing, yet to be numbered among David’s valiant men and set over a course is honour enough. The dictionary honours that Ira kept his month faithfully, watchful in his station as his name declares, neither slumbering nor forsaking his rank. The kingdom of David figures the kingdom of Christ, and they that serve the greater David are bidden to watch and be sober. Ira the watchful stands as a witness that the LORD honours the soldier who keeps his post, and that to be found watching when the Master cometh is the blessedness of His servants.

etymology: Hebrew ’abi‘ezer, “my father is help” or “father of help,” the Antothite, captain of the ninth monthly course of David’s host, one of the mighty men.
biblical_def: Abiezer the Antothite was set over the course of the ninth month in the ordering of David’s army, of four and twenty thousand men (1Ch 27:12). He is named among the mighty men of David in both rolls, called the Antothite or Anethothite, a man of Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, the town that in later days gave the prophet Jeremiah to Israel (1Ch 11:28; 2Sa 23:27). His name signifies “my father is help,” a confession built into the very name, declaring that help cometh not from the arm of flesh but from above. The dictionary honours that Abiezer, bearing so good a name, served faithfully in his appointed course, taking his month in the host of the anointed king. There is a doctrine folded into his name, for the soldier who knows that his father is help fights not in his own strength but leans upon the LORD his God. Of his own exploits the Scripture is silent, yet his name preaches what every saint must learn, that our help is in the name of the LORD who made heaven and earth. Abiezer stands as a witness that the warfare of the saints under Christ the greater David is waged in dependence and not in self-confidence, and that he serves best who reckons his strength to be the help of his God. The mighty man whose name confessed his help kept his rank, and so the saint who leans upon the LORD shall not be moved.

etymology: Hebrew sibbekay, “weaver” or “thicket of the LORD,” the Hushathite, captain of the eighth monthly course of David’s host, who slew the giant Saph.
biblical_def: Sibbecai the Hushathite was set over the course of the eighth month in the ordering of David’s army, of four and twenty thousand men, and he was of the Zarhites of the tribe of Judah (1Ch 27:11). He is renowned above the silent captains, for he slew Sippai, also called Saph, who was of the children of the giant, in the war with the Philistines at Gob or Gezer, and so the Philistines were subdued (1Ch 20:4; 2Sa 21:18). His name perhaps signifies “weaver,” yet his deed was the unmaking of a giant. The dictionary honours that Sibbecai both kept his appointed course in the host and went down to battle against the seed of the giants, those mighty enemies of the people of God. There is a figure here that warms the heart, for the giants were the terror of Israel, and the LORD raised up His servants to lay them low one by one. As David smote Goliath, so Sibbecai smote Saph, that the children of the giant might fall before the men of the anointed king. Sibbecai stands as a witness that the greater David, the Lord Jesus Christ, gives His soldiers the victory over the giant powers that defy His people, and that no enemy is too mighty to be subdued by the hand the LORD strengthens. The weaver’s son became a giant-slayer; so the LORD makes the lowly mighty for the casting down of strongholds.

biblical_def: Maharai the Netophathite was set over the course of the tenth month in the ordering of David’s army, of four and twenty thousand men, and he was of the Zarhites of the tribe of Judah (1Ch 27:13). His name signifies “swift,” a fitting word for a soldier ready and quick to the service of his lord, not slothful nor slow when the king commanded. The kingdom of David figures the kingdom of Christ, and they that serve the greater David are bidden to run with patience the race set before them, and to be swift to do the will of their Captain. Maharai the swift stands as a witness that the LORD honours the soldier who comes quickly to his post and lingers not, but is ready in the day of his appointed service.

The dictionary records him that the reader who meets the name among David’s mighty men may know him for a real soldier in a real host, of Netophah near Bethlehem, swift to his appointed course as his name declares.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the readiness that becomes a soldier of the King. He whose name means swift kept his month in David’s host, neither tardy nor reluctant in his rank. The saint bidden to make haste and delay not to keep the commandments may remember Maharai the swift, and learn that the LORD honours the servant who comes quickly to his post and is ready in the day of his appointed service.

etymology: Hebrew cheldai, “worldly” or “enduring, lasting,” the Netophathite, captain of the twelfth monthly course of David’s host, also called Heled and Heleb.
biblical_def: Heldai the Netophathite was set over the course of the twelfth month in the ordering of David’s army, of four and twenty thousand men, and he was of Othniel, a man of the stock of that first judge of Israel (1Ch 27:15). He is named among the mighty men of David, called Heled the son of Baanah the Netophathite in the Chronicler’s roll and Heleb in the book of Samuel, the same valiant man under the three forms of the name (1Ch 11:30; 2Sa 23:29). His name perhaps signifies “enduring,” a fitting word for the captain of the last month, who held the rear of the year’s long course. The dictionary honours that Heldai, however his name be spelled, served faithfully to the end, taking the twelfth and final month when the year was full and the labour nearly done. There is a comfort here for the saint who must serve to the last, for the captain of the twelfth month is an image of perseverance unto the end, when the race is nearly run and the crown is near. The kingdom of David figures the kingdom of Christ, and they that endure unto the end shall be saved. Heldai the enduring stands as a witness that the LORD honours the soldier who keeps his rank to the closing month, and that he who is faithful unto death shall receive the crown of life from the hand of the greater David.

etymology: Hebrew benayah, “the LORD hath built” or “built of the LORD,” the Pirathonite, of the children of Ephraim, captain of the eleventh monthly course of David’s host, one of the thirty.
biblical_def: Benaiah the Pirathonite, of the children of Ephraim, was set over the course of the eleventh month in the ordering of David’s army, of four and twenty thousand men (1Ch 27:14). He is named among the mighty men of David, a man of Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, and he is one of the thirty (1Ch 11:31; 2Sa 23:30). This Benaiah is to be carefully distinguished from Benaiah the son of Jehoiada the priest, that other and more famous Benaiah who was over David’s guard, who slew two lionlike men of Moab and went down and slew a lion in the midst of a pit in time of snow; the two men share a name only, not a history, and the reader must not confound them. His name signifies “the LORD hath built,” a word that confesses the LORD as the builder of His people and His kingdom. The dictionary honours that Benaiah the Pirathonite kept his appointed course in the host, an Ephraimite numbered among the thirty valiant of the king. There is a doctrine in his name, for except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Benaiah whom the LORD hath built stands as a witness that the soldiers of the anointed are themselves a building of God, fitly framed together and set each in his place, for the greater David builds His church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
